prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Kimi Raikkonen has lambasted McLaren's Lewis Hamilton for the pit-lane accident that ended both of their races at the Canadian Grand Prix. Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen is far from happy after Lewis Hamilton  pushed him out of the Canadian Grand Prix. Hamilton's McLaren rammed into the back of world champion Raikkonen's Ferrari as the Finn and Robert Kubica, the race's eventual winner, were waiting at a red light after the safety car was forced into action on lap 17. Raikkonen, while claiming not to be angry, was clearly far from impressed. "There's not much I can say. My race was ruined by Hamilton's mistake. "Obviously, anyone can make mistakes, as I did two weeks ago in Monaco, but it's one thing to make a mistake at 200 hundred [miles] per hour but another to hit a car stopped at a red light. "I'm not angry because that doesn't achieve anything and does not change my result. I am unhappy because I had a great chance of winning." Raikkonen, who has failed to score points in the previous two races, said he had to start winning again. "There is still a long way to go in the championship and it is still very close and we have everything we need to regain the ground we have lost." Ferrari team sporting director Stefano Domenicali said Hamilton had made a "serious mistake." "I think the penalty imposed by the FIA [Hamilton was given a 10-place grid penalty for the French Grand Prix at Magny-Cours] is in line with it, even if it does not restore what was a lost opportunity for us. "Kimi was in an excellent position to fight for the win" Hamilton, for his part, was apologetic. "I don't know what happened to be honest," Hamilton said. "I was comfortably in the lead, it was looking like an easy win. Then I went in for the pit stop. It was not a good stop and I saw the two guys in front of me battling in the pit lane. "I saw the red light but by that time it was a bit late. It was not exactly a racing incident as such, it was unfortunate. It was one of those things. It is different to if you crash into the wall and you are angry. It is not like that. I apologize to Kimi for ruining his race."

LONDON, England (CNN) — Kimi Raikkonen has sharply criticized McLaren’s Lewis Hamilton over the pit-lane collision that ended both drivers’ races at the Canadian Grand Prix.

Ferrari driver Raikkonen was far from pleased after Hamilton forced him out of the race. Hamilton’s McLaren struck the rear of the reigning world champion’s Ferrari as Raikkonen and Robert Kubica—the race’s eventual winner—waited at a red light after the safety car was deployed on lap 17.

Although Raikkonen insisted he was not angry, the Finn was clearly unimpressed.

“There’s not much I can say. My race was ruined by Hamilton’s mistake,” he said. “Obviously, anyone can make mistakes, as I did two weeks ago in Monaco, but it’s one thing to make a mistake at 200 miles per hour and another to hit a car stopped at a red light.

“I’m not angry because that doesn’t achieve anything and does not change my result. I am unhappy because I had a great chance of winning.”

Raikkonen, who has failed to score points in the past two races, said he needed to start winning again.

“There is still a long way to go in the championship, and it is still very close. We have everything we need to regain the ground we have lost.”

Ferrari sporting director Stefano Domenicali said Hamilton had made a “serious mistake.”

“I think the penalty imposed by the FIA”—Hamilton received a 10-place grid penalty for the French Grand Prix at Magny-Cours—“is in line with it, even if it does not restore what was a lost opportunity for us.

“Kimi was in an excellent position to fight for the win.”

Hamilton, for his part, was apologetic.

“I don’t know what happened, to be honest,” Hamilton said. “I was comfortably in the lead, and it was looking like an easy win. Then I went in for the pit stop. It was not a good stop, and I saw the two guys in front of me battling in the pit lane.

“I saw the red light, but by that time it was a bit late. It was not exactly a racing incident as such; it was unfortunate. It was one of those things. It is different from crashing into the wall and being angry. It is not like that. I apologize to Kimi for ruining his race.”

LONDON, England (CNN) — Kimi Raikkonen strongly criticized McLaren driver Lewis Hamilton after a pit-lane collision brought both men’s Canadian Grand Prix races to an end.

The incident occurred after the safety car was deployed on lap 17. Raikkonen and Robert Kubica—who went on to win the race—were stationary at a red light at the pit-lane exit when Hamilton’s McLaren struck the rear of the reigning world champion’s Ferrari.

Although Raikkonen insisted he was not angry, he made his dissatisfaction clear.

“There is not much to say. Hamilton’s error destroyed my race,” the Finnish driver said. “Of course, everybody makes mistakes. I made one myself in Monaco two weeks ago. But making an error at 200 miles per hour is very different from crashing into a car that is stopped at a red light.

“Being angry would accomplish nothing and would not alter the result. What disappoints me is that I had an excellent opportunity to win.”

Having scored no points in the last two races, Raikkonen said it was important for him to return to winning form.

“The championship still has a long way to run, the standings remain very tight, and we have everything required to recover the ground we have lost,” he said.

Ferrari sporting director Stefano Domenicali described Hamilton’s actions as a “serious mistake.”

He said the FIA’s punishment—a 10-position grid penalty for Hamilton at the French Grand Prix in Magny-Cours—was appropriate, although it could not compensate Ferrari for the missed opportunity.

“Kimi was in a very strong position to challenge for victory,” Domenicali added.

Hamilton, meanwhile, apologized for the collision.

“To be honest, I’m not sure what happened,” he said. “I had a comfortable lead, and it seemed as though the win would be straightforward. Then I came in for my pit stop. The stop was not good, and I saw the two drivers ahead of me fighting in the pit lane.

“I noticed the red light, but by then it was already a little too late. It was not really a racing incident; it was simply unfortunate—one of those things. It is different from crashing into a wall and feeling angry. This was not like that. I apologize to Kimi for ending his race.”

# Hamilton pit-lane crash clears path for Kubica’s historic Canadian GP win

**Montreal, June 8, 2008** — Robert Kubica claimed his maiden Formula One victory in a dramatic Canadian Grand Prix after Lewis Hamilton crashed into the back of Kimi Räikkönen at a red light in the pit lane.

The pivotal incident occurred during a safety-car period at the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve. Kubica and Räikkönen had completed their stops and reached the pit-lane exit side by side, where both halted because the light was red.

Hamilton, arriving behind them, failed to stop in time and struck the rear of Räikkönen’s Ferrari. Nico Rosberg then hit Hamilton’s McLaren in the resulting congestion.

Hamilton and Räikkönen retired immediately with substantial damage, while Rosberg continued after replacing his front wing. Kubica, who had been alongside Räikkönen but escaped contact, rejoined the race and went on to secure a landmark victory for BMW Sauber.

“It was a perfect day,” Kubica said after leading teammate Nick Heidfeld home for a BMW Sauber one-two. David Coulthard finished third for Red Bull.

The result carried particular significance for Kubica, whose frightening accident at the same circuit one year earlier had forced him to miss the following race. His Montreal triumph was the first Formula One victory for a Polish driver and BMW Sauber’s first — and ultimately only — Grand Prix win.

Hamilton accepted responsibility for the collision but said he had concentrated on the cars rather than the pit-exit signal.

“I saw the two cars battling in the pit lane and I saw the red light too late,” he said. “It’s not exactly a racing incident, but these things happen.”

Räikkönen, the reigning world champion, expressed frustration but remained restrained after being eliminated while stationary.

“There is not much I can say,” the Ferrari driver said. “I stopped because the light was red, and somebody hit me.”

Race officials later handed Hamilton a 10-place grid penalty for the following French Grand Prix. Rosberg received the same sanction for his role in the secondary impact.

Kubica’s victory moved him into the lead of the drivers’ championship after seven rounds, four points ahead of Hamilton and Felipe Massa. It also completed a remarkable turnaround at a circuit where, 12 months earlier, he had survived one of the most violent crashes of the modern Formula One era.

## Hamilton’s Pit-Lane Error Wrecks Räikkönen’s Canadian Grand Prix

**MONTREAL, June 8, 2008** — Lewis Hamilton’s bid for a second consecutive Canadian Grand Prix victory ended in a bizarre pit-lane collision when the McLaren driver rear-ended Kimi Räikkönen’s stationary Ferrari during a safety-car period at Circuit Gilles Villeneuve.

The incident occurred after Adrian Sutil’s stopped Force India prompted officials to deploy the safety car. Once the pit lane reopened, the leading drivers came in for fuel and tires, creating a rush of cars heading toward the pit exit.

Robert Kubica and Räikkönen completed their stops and raced side by side down the pit lane, but both drivers correctly stopped at the exit because the signal was red while the safety-car train passed on the circuit. Hamilton, leaving his McLaren pit box behind them, failed to slow in time and struck the rear of Räikkönen’s Ferrari.

Nico Rosberg, following in his Williams, then hit the back of Hamilton’s McLaren, adding to the confusion.

The impact eliminated both Hamilton and Räikkönen immediately. Rosberg was able to continue after returning to the pits for repairs, although his race was compromised.

Hamilton, who had started from pole position and led the early stages, said he noticed the red light but reacted too late after focusing on the two cars in front of him.

“I saw the two guys in front battling in the pit lane, and all of a sudden they stopped,” Hamilton said. “I saw the red light, but by then it was too late.”

The McLaren driver accepted responsibility for the mistake but described it as an unusual situation.

“It’s not exactly a racing incident as such, but these things happen,” he said. “I’m sorry for Kimi. I’ve apologized to him.”

Räikkönen was far less forgiving. The reigning world champion had been stationary and waiting legally at the signal when Hamilton’s car hit him from behind.

“There’s not much I can do when somebody hits me when I’m stopped at a red light,” Räikkönen said. “I don’t know what he was doing. You have to be able to see the red light and the cars stopped in front.”

The Ferrari driver called the accident especially frustrating because it occurred away from normal racing action.

“Mistakes happen, but it’s one thing to make a mistake at 200 kilometers an hour,” Räikkönen said. “It’s another to hit a car that is stopped at a red light.”

Race stewards later ruled that Hamilton and Rosberg had caused avoidable collisions. Both received 10-place grid penalties for the following French Grand Prix.

The crash transformed the race. With Hamilton and Räikkönen out, Kubica went on to claim his first Formula One victory and BMW Sauber’s first win, leading teammate Nick Heidfeld home for a one-two finish. The result also carried particular significance for Kubica, who had suffered a violent accident at the same circuit one year earlier.

For Hamilton, however, the afternoon was defined by a moment of inattention at the end of the pit lane—a low-speed mistake that ended the races of two championship contenders and produced one of the most memorable safety-car incidents of the 2008 season.
